findings.text: The v0.4 precedence rule sends a lane that sees LP-11 in DL_HS_RQST, DL_LP_RQST or DL_ESC_RQST through DL_ERR and back to DL_STOP on the same LP-11, while DL_ERR holds errcontrol_x 'until the next line-state change' [CSI] C13. The line stays LP-11, so it is not stated whether errcontrol_x stays high while the lane already reports Stop, or for how long.
findings.source_quote: that row takes precedence: the lane passes through DL_ERR, raising `errcontrol_x`, and then returns to DL_STOP ⚠️.
findings.proposed_default: errcontrol_x stays high until the next line-state change after that LP-11 (the next LP-01 or LP-10), per C13, while the lane is already in DL_STOP; confirm with the CSI team that a Stop state with errcontrol_x high is acceptable.

findings.text: HAS-CSI places rxsynchs_x in the cycle of the first payload byte in Table 4-4 (#8) and in its Lane Management text, but its Figure 4-1 draws the pulse one cycle before B1. The HAS-CSI write condition (rxvalidhs_x with sync_seen_x or rxsynchs_x) accepts both; this IP follows the table.
findings.source_quote: The lane management of the CSI-2 Rx controller writes a byte
findings.proposed_default: Follow HAS-CSI Table 4-4 (pulse in the cycle of B1); ask the CSI team to align Figure 4-1.

findings.text: The eot_skip_bytes formula of Table 3-2 adds the LP-11 detection latency and the crossing of the EoT request, but not the latency of the data path (the word latency Λ of §5.2 and the alignment register). When the request arrives, the newest delay-line entries hold the line about Λ + 1 byte clocks earlier than the formula assumes, so the cut may fall that much early. Not yet checked with an EoT model.
findings.source_quote: `eot_skip_bytes` places the cut between 40 ns and THS-TRAIL,min before LP-11
findings.proposed_default: Keep the formula; check the cut with an EoT model of the delay line (ADR-006) before the RTL, then add Λ to the formula if the model confirms the offset.
